post.title: WarpAxe 0.1.50 Adds Voltage-Regulator Cooling and Fan Failure Protection to Bitcoin Miners
post.content:
Open-source Bitcoin mining firmware WarpAxe introduced an additional thermal-control loop in its November 27, 2026 release. Version 0.1.50 adds regulator temperature to automatic fan control on supported single-fan boards, expands startup protection against unavailable fan controllers and provides fixed IPv4 addressing with automatic recovery. The changes concern operating reliability rather than new ASIC silicon or a demonstrated improvement in joules per terahash. They follow the earlier WarpAxe networking and fan-control update.

Why a cool ASIC can coexist with a hot regulator

A mining board converts input electrical power into the low-voltage, high-current supply required by its hashing chips. Switching regulators lose some energy in transistors, inductors and other components. A heatsink mounted on an ASIC may keep its junction temperature within the expected range while the separate power-conversion stage experiences higher thermal stress. Texas Instruments' technical discussion of thermally optimized power supplies illustrates why regulator losses and heat dissipation matter when powering processors.

Consider an illustrative regulator supplying 40 W to a chip rail. At 95% conversion efficiency, the input is 42.11 W and regulator losses are 2.11 W. At 90%, input increases to 44.44 W and losses rise to 4.44 W. A five-percentage-point efficiency reduction more than doubles the heat released by the regulator in the example. These figures are not measurements of the Bitaxe Naja Duo or another specific board. Actual losses depend on voltage, current, switching conditions and component characteristics.

Two thermal inputs instead of one

The new automatic cooling logic selects the higher fan demand from the hashing-chip and regulator control loops. The regulator's default target is 80°C; the previous release notes describe a 105°C protective stop. Supported NerdQAxe, NerdOCTAXE and NerdQX boards also inhibit hashing if their fan controller fails initialization three times. Earlier November 23 firmware introduced comparable protection for certain other boards and checks for unexpected regulator configuration resets.

These are firmware control thresholds, not universal safe operating temperatures or a recommendation to increase voltage. The developer reports that six test boards did not reach the new regulator target during normal operation; consequently, their fan speeds did not change. No independent thermal-stress comparison or fleet-wide efficiency gain has been demonstrated. Our explanation of nameplate and wall-level mining efficiency describes why cooling overhead and measurement boundaries must be included in performance comparisons.

Reliability extends beyond hashing

The release also introduces optional static IPv4 addressing with a recovery mechanism that returns to automatic address allocation after three minutes without evidence of connectivity. For small mining fleets, dependable telemetry and access can matter as much as peak hashrate. The recent HashedMax pool closure notice illustrates another dimension of infrastructure dependence. Operators should use supported hardware, verified firmware releases and appropriate cooling, monitoring both accepted pool work and electrical consumption. The engineering goal is stable useful computation, not simply a higher reported clock speed.
